activities.anchor: A rotting log is a continent at insect scale
activities.caption: call the magnitude — just the ants
activities.name: idmAntsEstimate

config.prompt: A 2022 study put a number on ants alone — roughly how many individual ants are alive on Earth?
config.why: About 20 quadrillion ants — with a total biomass exceeding that of all wild birds and wild mammals combined.
config.context: All insects together: some ten quintillion individuals — numbers that leave the human scale behind entirely.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the arthropod character list
activities.name: idmCharsSpot

config.prompt: A student's summary of the five arthropod characters contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: The body is segmented, with segments grouped into functional regions — tagmosis.
Each segment carries paired, jointed appendages that evolution can retool freely.
The whole animal is wrapped in an exoskeleton: chitin stiffened with protein.
Because armour cannot stretch, growth happens gradually inside the same cuticle.
Blood washes freely through the body cavity in an open circulatory system.
config.correction: Because armour cannot stretch, arthropods must moult — periodically shedding the cuticle (ecdysis), expanding briefly, and re-hardening.
config.why: The exoskeleton is armour that must be shed to grow — the trade-off that steers every discrete instar later in the subject.

activities.caption: file each creature by its branch
activities.name: idmBranchBuckets

config.prompt: Legs, antennae, sections — file each creature by its arthropod branch:

items.label: spider — four leg pairs, no antennae, two body regions
woodlouse — two pairs of antennae, mostly watery homes
centipede — dozens to hundreds of legs, one or two pairs per segment
housefly — exactly six legs, one antenna pair, three sections

config.why: The leg count is the fastest identification habit you can build: most misidentifications end before they start.

activities.anchor: the first animals on Earth to do so
activities.caption: put flight's debut on the timeline
activities.name: idmFlightPlace

config.prompt: Insects beat every vertebrate into the air. About how many million years ago was that?
config.why: By the Carboniferous, about 350 million years ago — roughly 150 million years before any flying vertebrate, and never lost once invented.

activities.anchor: That same Carboniferous air was rich in oxygen
activities.caption: the O₂ ceiling — drag from coal swamps to today
activities.name: idmO2Compare

config.prompt: Atmospheric oxygen, then and now — drag the divider:

before.label: coal-swamp era
before.text: Perhaps 30–35% O₂ — the size ceiling rose, and Meganeura, a dragonfly relative with a wingspan near 70 centimetres, patrolled the swamps.

after.label: today
after.text: About 21% O₂ — diffusion through tracheal tubes caps body size, and the giants went with the decline.

config.why: The atmosphere sets a hard ceiling on insect body size — a ceiling that rose and fell with it.

activities.anchor: Pollination bound the two lineages together
activities.caption: fill the blanks — one genome, two niches
activities.name: idmMetaCloze

config.text: The Holometabola — beetles, flies, wasps and bees, butterflies and moths — evolved the complete life cycle: a worm-like %%0%% dissolves in the %%1%% and rebuilds as an adult. Because the young never compete with their own %%2%%, one genome exploits two niches: a caterpillar strips leaves while its butterfly sips nectar.
config.hint: Roughly two-thirds of all insect species — including the beetles, with some 350,000–400,000 described species — hold this trick.

activities.anchor: The fourth move is the least glamorous
activities.caption: bet before you read on — who rebounds?
activities.name: idmReboundPredict

config.q: A catastrophe kills 99% of an insect population — and, in a parallel world, 99% of a large, slow-breeding mammal population. Which species rebounds?
choices: The mammal — bigger bodies, better odds
The insect — breeding rate is extinction insurance
Neither — a 99% loss is terminal for both
config.why: Small bodies mature fast and breed in enormous numbers: populations rebound from catastrophes that would end a species of large, slow-breeding animals.

activities.anchor: One appendage set, a dozen professions
activities.caption: pair each mouthpart with its profession
activities.name: idmMouthMatch

config.prompt: The ancestral chewing mouthparts, re-engineered — pair modification with owner:
config.why: The mouthpart type alone will usually tell you an insect's order — structure is biography.
